title: Capstone: feed
summary: Choose fanout-on-write or fanout-on-read from follower shape; name the queue.

parts.rule: Design a social feed using only lessons already taught. Choose fanout-on-write (precompute timelines) versus fanout-on-read (pull from followees at read time) from follower and followee counts. If you precompute, name the work queue that performs fanout and the idempotent timeline write. Call out celebrity hot keys.
parts.why: Feeds are the classic tradeoff question. Blindly picking push or pull without numbers is a fail. The queue and the hot-key story show you understand write amplification versus read latency.
parts.example: Assumptions: average user has two hundred followees and two hundred followers; a celebrity has ten million followers. Fanout-on-write for normal users: on post, enqueue job that inserts (follower_id, post_id, ts) into each follower timeline; reads are a single timeline query by user_id ordered by ts. For celebrity posts, skip full fanout — readers merge the celebrity's recent posts at read time (hybrid). Numbers: average post touches two hundred timeline writes; at one thousand posts/sec that is two hundred thousand timeline writes/sec — needs batched consumers and sharding timelines by user_id. Fanout-on-read alone would query two hundred followee recent-post lists per feed load, fine for tiny graphs, painful at scale. Cache the home timeline for active users with invalidation on new fanout inserts. Name the force before the mechanism.
parts.use: Use this capstone to practice stating push versus pull with numbers. Use hybrid fanout when the follower distribution is skewed. Use the work-queue lesson for the push path.
parts.refuse: Refuse pure fanout-on-write to ten million followers on the request thread. Refuse pure fanout-on-read for dense graphs without a latency budget. Refuse a feed design with no queue and no hot-key plan. Refuse inventing a new storage paradigm outside the track.

body:
Rule. Design a social feed using only lessons already taught. Choose fanout-on-write (precompute timelines) versus fanout-on-read (pull from followees at read time) from follower and followee counts. If you precompute, name the work queue that performs fanout and the idempotent timeline write. Call out celebrity hot keys.

Why it matters. Feeds are the classic tradeoff question. Blindly picking push or pull without numbers is a fail. The queue and the hot-key story show you understand write amplification versus read latency.

Worked example. Assumptions: average user has two hundred followees and two hundred followers; a celebrity has ten million followers. Fanout-on-write for normal users: on post, enqueue job that inserts (follower_id, post_id, ts) into each follower timeline; reads are a single timeline query by user_id ordered by ts. For celebrity posts, skip full fanout — readers merge the celebrity's recent posts at read time (hybrid). Numbers: average post touches two hundred timeline writes; at one thousand posts/sec that is two hundred thousand timeline writes/sec — needs batched consumers and sharding timelines by user_id. Fanout-on-read alone would query two hundred followee recent-post lists per feed load, fine for tiny graphs, painful at scale. Cache the home timeline for active users with invalidation on new fanout inserts. Name the force before the mechanism.

When to use. Use this capstone to practice stating push versus pull with numbers. Use hybrid fanout when the follower distribution is skewed. Use the work-queue lesson for the push path.

When to refuse. Refuse pure fanout-on-write to ten million followers on the request thread. Refuse pure fanout-on-read for dense graphs without a latency budget. Refuse a feed design with no queue and no hot-key plan. Refuse inventing a new storage paradigm outside the track.
